q.intro.text: Sneakers are marked sixty dollars. The sales tax is eight percent.

q.ask.text: What do you pay at the register?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: The shelf price, sixty dollars, is before tax. It is the whole: one hundred percent. The tape is the same sixty dollars.

e.s2.text: One percent of sixty dollars is sixty cents. So eight percent is eight times sixty cents: four dollars and eighty cents. The tax sticks out past the hundred percent.

e.s3.text: Sixty dollars plus four eighty is sixty-four dollars and eighty cents. That is the total, what you pay.

e.s4.text: The total is one hundred percent plus eight percent: one hundred eight percent of the price. One point zero eight times sixty dollars is sixty-four eighty: the same total, in one step.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does one point zero eight times sixty dollars give the total?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The one keeps the whole price, and the point zero eight adds the tax: one hundred eight percent of the price.

e.w-less.text: A percent can be more than one hundred percent. The total is the price and more: one hundred eight percent of it.

e.w-append.text: It is not about the digits. Eight percent is point zero eight, so the multiplier is one plus point zero eight. For seven and a half percent tax it is one point zero seven five, not one point seven five.

t.intro.text: Now a forty dollar board game with seven and a half percent tax. The first two steps are done for you.

t.tax.text: The tax: seven and a half percent is point zero seven five, and that times forty dollars is three dollars.

t.add.text: Your step: what do you pay in total?

t.empty.text: Type an amount, like twelve fifty.

t.a-ok.text: Yes: forty dollars plus three dollars is forty-three dollars.

t.a-pct.text: That adds seven dollars and fifty cents. The tax is seven and a half percent of the price: three dollars.

t.a-tax.text: Three dollars is the tax. You pay the price and the tax.

t.a-sub.text: Sales tax is added at the register, not taken off.

t.a-shelf.text: The forty dollars on the shelf is before tax. The tax comes on top.

t.a-other.text: Add the tax to the pre-tax price: forty dollars plus three dollars.

t.mult.text: Your step: which one multiplication gives the total?

t.m-ok.text: Yes: one hundred percent plus seven and a half percent is one hundred seven and a half percent, so one point zero seven five times forty dollars is forty-three dollars.

t.m-append.text: Seven and a half percent is point zero seven five, so the multiplier is one plus point zero seven five. One point seven five times forty dollars would be seventy dollars.

t.m-tax.text: Point zero seven five times forty dollars is only the tax, three dollars. The total keeps the price too.

t.m-down.text: Point nine two five takes seven and a half percent off, like a discount. Tax is added.

t.bench.text: Last check: is three dollars a sensible tax on forty dollars?

t.b-ok.text: Five percent of forty dollars is two dollars, and ten percent is four dollars. Seven and a half percent is between them, and so is three dollars.

t.b-one.text: Less than forty dollars is only one side: thirty dollars is less than forty too. Check a lower and an upper bound.

t.b-scale.text: Thirty dollars would be seventy-five percent of the price. Ten percent is only four dollars, so the tax is under four dollars.

t.cb-68.text: At the start you picked sixty-eight dollars. That adds eight dollars, but eight percent of sixty dollars is four eighty.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked sixty-four eighty, and you were right. Now you can show why: the price is one hundred percent, the total one hundred eight.

t.cb-480.text: At the start you picked four eighty. That is the tax. You pay the price and the tax.

t.cb-none.text: The pre-tax price is one hundred percent. The tax adds its percent on top, so the total is more than one hundred percent of the price.

p.intro.text: Ana’s receipt says the total is eighty-one dollars, with eight percent tax, but the price is torn off. Ana says: eight percent of eighty-one dollars is six forty-eight, so the price was seventy-four dollars and fifty-two cents. Is Ana right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: The total, eighty-one dollars, is one hundred eight percent of the pre-tax price, because the price is the whole and the tax adds eight percent on top.

p.c2.text: So the price is eighty-one dollars divided by one point zero eight: seventy-five dollars, and the tax is six dollars, because dividing by one point zero eight undoes the times one point zero eight.

p.c3.text: And Ana’s six forty-eight is too much, because eighty-one dollars is a bigger whole than seventy-five, so each percent of it is bigger.

p.x-cancel.text: They do not cancel. The eight percent added was of seventy-five dollars. The eight percent Ana takes off is of eighty-one dollars, a bigger whole.

p.x-div.text: Eighty-one dollars divided by point zero eight is over a thousand dollars: far too much. Point zero eight times the price is only the tax. The total is one point zero eight times the price.

p.x-dollars.text: Eight percent is not eight dollars. The tax was eight percent of the price.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the tapes back every one. Undo a tax by dividing by one point zero eight, not by taking eight percent of the total.
